title: Krishna Retrieves Sandipani's Son
story:
Krishna and his elder brother Balarama had spent their student years far from home, at the school of the sage Sandipani in the city of Avanti. When their studies were done, they went to their teacher and asked what fee he would take. It was the custom: at the end of his studies a student offers his teacher whatever is asked of him, for a student's debt is not discharged with words. The two brothers had learned the whole Veda, the sacred scriptures, at Sandipani's feet, and they meant to pay their debt in full.

Sandipani had taught them as he would teach any boy, holding nothing back, and now he told them what he wanted. It was not gold, or cattle, or land. Long ago, he said, his young son had died in the sea at Prabhasa and had never come home. He had spoken of it with his wife first, for the request was not a small one; it reached back into a grief that had never healed. "Give me back my son," he said. It was a fee no one else in the world could pay. Krishna agreed at once.

Krishna and Balarama mounted their chariot and drove to Prabhasa, to the very shore where the boy had been lost. It was a long road, but they did not linger on it; a teacher's word had set them moving, and they meant to see it done. The shore was empty, and the waves came up the sand and fell back again, as if the sea were waiting to see what they would ask. Then the ocean itself rose, for it knew who had come, and brought them an offering and asked what they sought. "The son of our teacher," Krishna said. "Give him back to us."

But the sea answered that the boy was not in its keeping. "A demon named Panchajana," it said, "lives in these waters in the form of a conch shell, and it was he who carried the boy off." The sea spoke plainly, unwilling to be blamed for what another had done.

At these words Krishna went down into the water without a moment's hesitation — down into the cold and the dark where the demon lay coiled in its shell — while Balarama waited on the shore above. He found Panchajana in the depths and killed him, and from the demon's body, for Panchajana was a monster shaped like a conch, he drew out the great shell itself. That shell was the conch the world would come to know as Panchajanya, named for the demon from whose form it was taken. Then he climbed back into the chariot, the conch in his hand, and with Balarama beside him he drove to the city of Yama, the lord of death.

The city of the dead is not reached by any road of the living, but at its gates Krishna raised the conch and blew it, and the sound of Panchajanya rolled through the realm of the dead like a summons no one there could refuse. Yama himself came out to meet them and honored them with deep reverence, and the boy — the teacher's son, dead and lost — was given back to the two brothers, brought back from death itself. Death, which had held him so long, gave him up without an argument.

They drove back to the hermitage with the boy alive again, seated in the chariot between them, and laid him in his father's arms — restored in his former person, as he had been before the sea took him, with no mark of death upon him. A father's long grief ended in a single afternoon. Sandipani, holding his son, blessed the two brothers and sent them on their way. "Go home, heroes," he said, "and may your fame be pure."
reflection: The story is unusual among the tales of Krishna's deeds because he appears in it as a student repaying a teacher, not as a king or a warrior. The fee Sandipani names — the life of his son — is one that no wealth could settle, and Krishna treats it as a debt he is glad to pay, going as far as the realm of death itself to honor a teacher's word.
content_note: Krishna slays the sea-demon Panchajana; the death is described briefly and without detail.
hero_scene: Krishna stands at the gates of Yama's dark city, raising the great conch Panchajanya to his lips, while Balarama waits at his side and the sound of the conch rolls out through the realm of death.
visual_elements: the demon Panchajana in the deep
